title: Belief Drives Behavior
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart distills a year of reading on noncognitive factors into one claim: belief drives behavior. He identifies five beliefs that multiply the growth students get from rigorous reading, writing and arguing: that the teacher is credible, that the student belongs, that effort improves ability, that the student can succeed, and that the work has value. The first comes from Hattie's Visible Learning, and the other four from Farrington et al.'s Teaching Adolescents to Become Learners. He insists the beliefs must be operational, held at the level of how students act, not merely intellectually assented to. He notes that the first belief is inward facing, since teachers cannot simply tell students to believe in them, while the others can be cultivated openly. He credits the researchers with turning sprawling jargon into clear statements.
points: Five student beliefs act as levers that multiply the effect of knowledge-rich, argument-steeped instruction.
Teacher credibility, per Hattie, makes it easier for students to listen, learn and persist.
Belonging works through identity, since students do what people like them do in this class.
Effort attribution and self-efficacy determine whether students see any point in working hard.
The beliefs must be operational rather than merely professed to have the multiplying effect.
quotes: Quite simply, when students believe certain things — believe them not merely at the “Yes, I intellectually assent to these statements” level but at the “I operate from these statements” level — about the reading or writing or speaking or arguing we ask them to do in our classes, then those activities will reap far more growth than they would otherwise. The right beliefs have a multiplying effect on the kinds of knowledge-rich, argument-steeped curricula we're trying to deliver each year.

In Hattie's work, this “I believe in my teacher” thing is called teacher credibility. When we can say with confidence that “this teacher is good at her job,” it's easier to listen, easier to learn, easier to muster the gumption required to grow.

Basically, it's easier to do things that line up with how we fancy ourselves: if I fancy myself a reader, I won't need to put too much effort into getting myself to read; if I think of myself as someone who doesn't read, however, I'll certainly find it difficult to want to read or to read effortfully. In short, we need our students to affirm that “people like us do things like we do in this class.

When we believe that some people are just born good at school and others aren't — when that's our highest internal principle for how school works — then there's not much incentive to work hard. “If I'm to get better, then it's up to me.

Commonly called self-efficacy or confidence, this should ring true to our own experience. When's the last time you were heavily motivated to do something at which you felt there was zero chance of success?
All of us have worked on these things in our classrooms for years. What Hattie and Farrington et al. have done for us is to make them clear, jargon-free statements. Big kudos to them.
